text: For a long time, scientists thought chameleons changed colour by spreading out or bunching up [[pigment|pigments]] in their skin, like ink spreading on paper. In 2015, researchers at the University of Geneva found that the real trick is far cleverer.

Under a chameleon's outer skin is a layer of cells called iridophores. These are packed with tiny [[crystal|crystals]] of a substance called guanine, arranged in a neat grid. When the chameleon relaxes, the crystals sit close together and reflect blue light, which mixes with yellow pigment above to look green. When it gets excited, the skin stretches, the crystals spread apart and they reflect yellow, orange and red instead.

st.prompt: A calm green panther chameleon meets a rival male. What happens to its colour?

options.t: It turns bright yellow, orange or red to look bigger and bolder
It turns the colour of the branch to hide

st.reveal: Excited males stretch the crystal layer in their skin, which reflects longer wavelengths of light. Their green turns yellow, orange or red, a signal that says "back off". The calmer, less colourful one usually leaves.

myth: Chameleons change colour to match whatever background they are on.

Chameleons are naturally well camouflaged, but they don't copy backgrounds. A chameleon on a red cloth won't turn red. They change colour mostly to send signals to other chameleons, to show their mood, and to control their temperature.

sec.t:
Chameleons mostly change colour to communicate. A male panther chameleon facing a rival turns from green to bright yellow or orange in a minute or two. The brightest, fastest-changing male usually wins without a fight.

Females use colour to say "not interested" to males, often turning dark with bright spots. Chameleons darken when cold, because dark skin soaks up more sunlight, and turn paler when hot. A sick or stressed chameleon may go dull and dark. So a chameleon's skin works more like a mood display than an [[@future-invisibility|invisibility cloak]].

A chameleon's tongue is another superpower. It can shoot out more than its own body length and grab an insect in a fraction of a second. Small chameleons have the fastest tongues for their size. In 2016, a scientist filmed one tiny [[species|species]], Rhampholeon spinosus, and found its tongue sped up at more than 250 times the pull of [[gravity|gravity]]. A fighter pilot blacks out at about 9.

The tongue works like a catapult. Muscles squeeze around an elastic sheath, storing energy, then let go all at once. The sticky tip grips prey with [[mucus|mucus]] far thicker than human [[saliva|saliva]].

Chameleon eyes sit in turret-like cones and can move separately. One can look forward while the other looks behind. When it spots food, both eyes swivel to lock on, judging distance for the strike.

There are more than 200 species. Nearly half live on the island of [[@madagascar|Madagascar]]. One of them, Brookesia nana, described in 2021, has males about 2 cm long including the tail, small enough to sit on a fingertip. India has the Indian chameleon, which lives in dry forests and scrubland from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu and in Sri Lanka.

sec.h: Masters of colour, but not the only ones
sec.t: Chameleons aren't the fastest colour changers. Their change takes a minute or two, and only some species, like the panther chameleon, put on dazzling shows. Cuttlefish and octopuses can change in less than a second, using muscles to stretch pigment sacs. Stranger still, octopuses seem to do it while being colourblind, a puzzle that keeps scientists studying [[@octopus-colour|how an octopus changes colour]].

text: No, not in the way most people mean. The red panda is not a bear, and it is not closely related to the giant panda. It belongs to a family all of its own, and its nearest living relatives are raccoons, skunks and weasels.

But here is the twist. The red panda had the name first. A French scientist described it for Europeans in 1825 and called it a panda. The giant panda wasn't described by Western scientists until 1869, and only later came to share the red panda's name.
So if anyone has a right to the name, it's the little red one.

sec.t:
A red panda is about the size of a house cat, with a long, bushy tail ringed in red and cream. Its face is white and rusty red, with tear-like stripes running down from its eyes. Its fur is thick and reddish, which helps it blend in with the reddish moss and lichen on the trees where it lives.

Red pandas live in cool, misty mountain forests in the eastern Himalayas and southwest [[@china-today|China]]. In India they are found in [[@sikkim|Sikkim]], where they are the state animal, in the Darjeeling hills of West Bengal and in Arunachal Pradesh.

They spend much of their time in trees. They can even climb down head first, turning their ankles around to grip the trunk. In cold weather they curl up on a branch and wrap their tail around themselves like a blanket.

Both kinds of panda face the same problem: holding a stalk of [[@bamboo|bamboo]]. Both solved it the same way. Each has a bone in its wrist that has grown long and sticks out like an extra thumb. They press the bamboo against it to grip.

Yet the two animals are only distant relatives. They [[evolve|evolved]] their false thumbs separately, because they ate the same food. Scientists call this convergent [[evolution|evolution]]: different animals arriving at the same answer to the same problem.

Red panda relatives once lived far beyond Asia. [[fossil|Fossils]] of a red panda cousin about 5 million years old have been found in Tennessee, in the USA.

In 2020, a team of Chinese scientists compared the DNA of red pandas from different areas. They found two groups that had been separated for a very long time, divided roughly by a big river in Arunachal Pradesh. They suggested calling them the Himalayan red panda and the Chinese red panda.

Not every expert agrees that they are different [[species|species]]. The debate matters, because if there are two, each has fewer animals and may need its own protection plan.

Red pandas are [[endangered|endangered]]. Their forests are being cut down for timber, farms and roads, and stray dogs can spread disease to them. Some are caught for the illegal pet trade.

The Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park in Darjeeling breeds red pandas and has released some into the forests of Singalila [[@national-parks|National Park]] nearby. In [[@nepal|Nepal]], local villagers are trained as "forest guardians" who track red pandas and protect their trees. Good [[@zoos-sanctuaries|zoos]] around the world, including in the USA, share animals to keep a healthy backup population.

text: A fire is a fast chemical reaction called [[combustion|combustion]]. It needs heat, fuel and oxygen, a trio firefighters call the fire triangle. Take away any one side and the flames die.

A fire extinguisher is a metal can full of something that attacks one side of that triangle. Water cools the fuel below the temperature where it can burn. [[carbon-dioxide|Carbon dioxide]] and foam smother the flames so oxygen cannot reach them. Dry powder gets in the way of the chemical reaction itself. Inside the can, gas under high [[pressure|pressure]] waits to blast the contents out the moment you squeeze the handle.

st.prompt: A carbon dioxide extinguisher puts out a fire mainly by doing what?

options.t: Pushing away the oxygen around the flames
Soaking the fuel with water
Freezing the fire solid

st.reveal: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air. It blankets the flames and pushes away the oxygen they need. It also cools things a little as it rushes out, but smothering is the main trick.

sec.h: What is inside the red can

sec.t:
Firefighters sort fires into classes. Burning wood, paper and cloth can be cooled with water. Burning petrol, oil or paint needs foam or powder, because water just floats the burning liquid around. Fires in electrical equipment need something that does not carry electricity, like CO₂ or powder.

Kitchen fires get their own class. A pan of oil can reach over 300°C. A splash of water sinks, boils instantly and throws burning oil into the air. Wet chemical extinguishers instead spray a liquid that reacts with the hot fat to form a soapy crust on top, sealing off the air. The lid that cooks are taught to slide over a small pan fire, one of the first rules of [[@kitchen-safety|kitchen safety]], works on the same smothering idea.

Small extinguishers empty fast, often in under 20 seconds. So people are trained to use them with a simple method, remembered as PASS. Pull the pin. Aim at the base of the fire, where the fuel is, not at the dancing flames on top. Squeeze the handle. Sweep from side to side.

Extinguishers are for small fires that have just started. If a fire is spreading, the right move is to get out and call the fire service: 101 or 112 in India, 911 in the USA. Using one is a job for adults. Children should leave, raise the alarm and, if anyone is burned, let a grown-up start [[@first-aid|first aid]] with cool running water.

sec.h: A short history of putting fires out
sec.t:
For most of history, fires were fought with buckets passed hand to hand. In 1723, a chemist in London named Ambrose Godfrey patented a device that used a small explosion to scatter fire-fighting liquid. It was clever but dangerous.

The ancestor of today's extinguisher came in 1818. George Manby, an English captain, had watched firefighters struggle to reach the upper floors of a burning building in Edinburgh. He designed a copper can holding about 13 litres of water with compressed air above it. Ordinary people could carry it to a fire. Since then the chemicals have changed, but the idea of squashed gas pushing out something that breaks the [[@fire-burns|fire triangle]] has stayed the same. Some homes now also keep a fire blanket, which is just that idea folded up in a pouch.

text: Most body scanners at airports today are millimetre-wave scanners. When you step inside and raise your arms, two panels sweep around you. They send out very weak radio waves, a bit like the waves your phone uses, but at a higher frequency. The waves pass through clothes but bounce off skin, and off anything hidden on top of it.

A computer measures the echoes and builds a 3D map of your outline in about two seconds. Software looks for anything that shouldn't be there, such as metal, plastic or powder. If it finds something, it marks the spot on a cartoon figure, and a security officer checks just that area.

So it can measure your height

st.reveal: The scanner's arms sweep around you sending and catching waves. Raised arms leave no hidden spots, so the computer can spot anything tucked against your sides.

d.try: Make a hidden-object test with a magnet on a string. Ask a friend to hide paper clips, coins and a plastic button inside socks. Dangle the magnet over each sock. Which items does it find, and which slip past? That's why airports use more than one kind of machine.
myth: Airport body scanners blast you with harmful radiation.

sec.t:
Radio waves come in many sizes. Your FM radio uses waves several metres long. Wi-Fi uses waves about 12 centimetres long. Body scanners use waves around a centimetre long or shorter, which scientists call millimetre waves.

Waves this size slip through cotton and wool like light through glass. But skin is full of water, and water reflects them. Metal reflects them strongly. Plastic, ceramic and powder reflect them differently from skin. By comparing the echoes, the computer spots the odd shape out. These are the same family of [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] that carry cricket commentary to a car radio, just much shorter.

Some airports still use the older walk-through metal detector, an arch that beeps when you forget your belt. It works with [[@magnets-how|magnetism]]. Coils in the arch send out short magnetic pulses hundreds of times a second.

When a pulse hits metal, it makes tiny electric currents swirl inside the metal. Those currents create their own faint magnetic field, which the coils pick up. A big enough echo means a beep. That's why coins and keys set it off, but a plastic comb does not.

The weakness is obvious. A metal detector can't find a ceramic knife or a packet of powder. Body scanners were brought in to close that gap. The scanners also have limits. They only see what sits on the skin, not inside the body, and loose or thick clothing, a bandage or a hair clip can trigger a quick check. A false alarm is common, and it doesn't mean anyone thinks you've done something wrong.

{{story:metal-detectors}}

The first body scanners used weak X-rays that bounced off the skin. They showed a ghostly picture of the person's body. Many travellers felt that was too personal, and some worried about [[radiation|radiation]], even though the dose was tiny. In 2013, the US removed them from its airports.

Now scanners use software called automatic target recognition. The officer never sees an image of you, just a standard outline, the same for everyone, with boxes showing where to look.

Your bags take a different trip. They ride through an [[@x-rays|X-ray]] machine that shows what's inside in false colours. Organic things like food and plastic often appear orange, metals blue or green, and everything else in between.

Newer CT scanners, like hospital scanners, take hundreds of X-ray slices and build a 3D picture. That's why some airports in India, the US and Europe now let you leave laptops and liquids inside your bag. Machines can even recognise the chemical "fingerprint" of some explosives.

For all this technology, some of the best detectors at an airport have four legs. Sniffer dogs can pick out tiny traces of explosives, drugs and even fruit hidden in luggage. A dog's [[@power-dogs-nose|nose]] has hundreds of millions of scent [[sensor|sensors]], compared with about 5 or 6 million in yours, and no machine has quite caught up.

text: Mix cornflour with water and you get a strange goo. It isn't quite a liquid or a solid. Its behaviour depends on how hard and fast you push it.

The mixture is made of countless tiny grains of [[starch|starch]] floating in water. When you move slowly, the water acts like a lubricant, and the grains slide easily past each other. The goo pours like thick cream. But when you hit it, squeeze it or stir it fast, the grains are forced together faster than the water can get out of the way. They jam into a tight, solid clump, and the mixture suddenly feels hard.
Scientists call this a shear-thickening liquid. Many children know it as oobleck.

st.reveal: A sudden, hard push jams the cornflour grains together so the mixture behaves like a solid for a moment. Your hand stays dry and bounces off. Push slowly, and the grains have time to slide past each other, so it flows like a liquid.

myth: Quicksand can suck you under and drown you.

People float in quicksand because the human body is less dense than the wet sand. You might sink to your waist and get stuck, but not go under. Getting out means moving slowly to let water back in around your legs.

sec.t:
In the late 1600s, the English scientist [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]] described how ordinary liquids flow. Water, oil and honey each have a fixed thickness, or viscosity, at a given temperature. Stir water gently or wildly and it stays just as runny. Honey gets runnier when you warm it, but stirring it faster doesn't change how thick it is.

Liquids that follow this rule are called Newtonian. Liquids that break it are called non-Newtonian. Their thickness changes depending on the force on them. Cornflour slime gets thicker when you push it hard. Others do the opposite.

sec.h: A name from a children's book

sec.t:
Because oobleck turns solid under sudden force, people have tried running across pools of it, often for science shows on television. Each footstep slams down hard, so the surface firms up and holds them for a moment. As long as they keep running, they stay on top.

If they stop, the grains relax, the mixture turns liquid again, and their feet slowly sink. Pulling a foot out quickly is hard, because the fast tug makes the goo grip again. The only way out is to move gently. Engineers have tested similar liquids for flexible body armour that stiffens on impact.

Some liquids do the opposite and get runnier when pushed. [[@food-ketchup-history|Ketchup]], made from [[@tomatoes|tomatoes]], is one. It sits stubbornly in the bottle until you shake or tap it hard, then suddenly rushes out. Paint is another. It spreads smoothly under a brush, but stays put on the wall without dripping.

Quicksand is a non-Newtonian mixture too, of sand, clay and water. It looks solid until you step on it, then it turns soft and swallows your feet. In 2005, scientists in Amsterdam showed in tests that a person can't sink completely, because the body is less dense than the sand. Films love scenes of people disappearing into quicksand, but in real life you'd float about waist-deep, stuck but safe. Some ordinary-looking [[@sand-where|sand]], it turns out, has a hidden liquid side.

text: Some tunes are catchy because they fit how our brains like to remember things. They tend to be simple, repeat a lot and follow a familiar shape, usually rising and then falling like a hill. But they also have one small surprise, such as an unexpected jump or a quirky [[rhythm|rhythm]], that makes the brain pay attention.

When a tune is easy to remember but slightly unusual, the brain keeps replaying it. Scientists call a song that loops in your head an earworm. Most people get one at least once a week. Film composers, advert makers and pop songwriters use these tricks on purpose.

st.prompt: In one study, what helped people stop a catchy song playing in their heads?

options.t: Chewing gum
Listening to the song ten more times
Standing on one foot

st.reveal: Researchers at the University of Reading found that chewing gum reduced how often people "heard" a catchy song in their heads. Chewing seems to keep busy the same mouth and throat movements we use when we silently sing along.

Ask each person which one is still stuck in their head an hour later. Then look at the winner: is it short, repeated, or does it have a surprise jump?

sec.t:
In 1975, the composer John Williams wrote the music for *Jaws*, a film about a giant shark. The director, Steven Spielberg, reportedly laughed when he first heard it. It was just two low notes, side by side, played slowly and then faster and faster.

But it worked. The two notes sound like a heartbeat speeding up or something approaching. Simple music is easy to recognise in a split second. Decades later, people still hum those two notes as a joke when someone creeps up behind them.

In 2016, researchers in the UK asked 3,000 people which songs got stuck in their heads most often. Then they studied the music itself.

The catchiest songs usually had a fairly fast beat. Their melodies followed shapes common in Western pop, rising then falling, but they also had unusual intervals, meaning surprise jumps between notes. Lady Gaga's "Bad Romance" topped the list.

Repetition matters too. The more often you hear a song, the more firmly your [[@memory|memory]] stores it. A chorus repeated four times in a song, and the song played every day on the radio, adds up fast.

{{story:music-brain}}

An earworm is usually only a short piece of a song, often 10 to 20 seconds of the chorus. It loops because the brain likes to finish things. If you hear part of a tune and it stops, your mind may keep playing it, trying to complete it.

Earworms often appear when your mind is relaxed or doing something easy, like walking or brushing teeth. They can also be set off by a word, a smell or a place linked to the song.

Advertisers know catchy tunes sell things. A short jingle linked to a brand name can stay with people for years. Many Indians can still hum old TV jingles from their childhood, along with the gentle signature tune of Doordarshan.

TV shows, sports events and news channels all use short theme tunes for the same reason. Hear a few notes and you know instantly what is coming. That's also why ringtones work. The Nokia tune, taken from a 1902 guitar waltz by Francisco Tárrega, became one of the most-played pieces of music in history.

In India, film songs are the national soundtrack. Composers such as [[@ar-rahman|A. R. Rahman]] build songs with strong hooks, memorable rhythms and surprising sounds. Many songs are heard first in a film, then at weddings, festivals and on phones for years.

A good hook in a film song works just like a hook in a story. It grabs you early and won't let go.

sec.h: How to get rid of one
sec.t:
Scientists have a few tips. Chewing gum may help, because it keeps your mouth too busy to silently sing along. Listening to the whole song all the way through can satisfy the brain's need to finish it. Some people swap in a different, "cure" song instead.

Music can do stranger things than loop in your head. At the best moment of a song, some people feel a shiver run down their spine, a reaction scientists call [[@music-goosebumps|music goosebumps]].

सबसे जाने-माने मणिपुरी नृत्य रासलीलाएँ हैं, जिनमें कृष्ण, राधा और गोपियों का प्रेम दिखाया जाता है। नर्तकियाँ *पोटलोई* नाम का कड़ा, चमकता, पीपे जैसा घाघरा पहनती हैं, जो शीशों और [[embroidery|कढ़ाई]] से सजा होता है, और साथ में एक महीन, पारदर्शी ओढ़नी। मणिपुरी में जोशीले ढोल नृत्य भी हैं, और मणिपुर के अपने मैतेई धर्म के देवताओं के लिए होने वाले कहीं पुराने नृत्य भी।

18वीं सदी में वैष्णव धर्म, यानी विष्णु और कृष्ण की उपासना, मणिपुर के राजदरबार का मुख्य धर्म बन गया। राजा भाग्यचंद्र, जिन्हें राजर्षि भाग्यचंद्र भी कहते हैं, को मणिपुरी रासलीला रचने का श्रेय दिया जाता है। परंपरा कहती है कि यह नृत्य और इसकी वेशभूषा उन्हें एक सपने में दिखी थी।

रासलीलाएँ पतझड़ और वसंत में पूनम की रातों को मंदिरों में होती हैं, और कई-कई घंटे चल सकती हैं। नर्तक अपने चेहरे शांत और सौम्य रखते हैं, कोई बड़े भाव नहीं दिखाते। भक्ति पूरे शरीर के बहाव से झलकती है।

मणिपुरी संगीत की अगुआई *पुंग* करता है, जो पीपे के आकार का एक [[@drums|ढोल]] है। *पुंग चोलोम* नाम के नृत्य में पुरुष ढोल वादक नर्तक भी बन जाते हैं। कंधों से ढोल लटकाए वे उछलते, उकड़ूँ बैठते, घूमते और चक्कर खाते हैं, और साथ-साथ पेचीदा [[rhythm|तालें]] बजाते रहते हैं।

झाँझ बजाने वाले *करताल चोलोम* में कुछ ऐसा ही करते हैं। ये नृत्य देखने में रोमांचक होते हैं और मणिपुरी का फुर्तीला, खिलाड़ियों वाला पहलू दिखाते हैं, वरना यह अपनी कोमलता के लिए जाना जाता है। इलाके की युद्ध-कला *थांग-ता* ने भी कुछ चालों पर असर डाला है।

1919 में कवि [[@tagore|रवींद्रनाथ टैगोर]] ने सिलहट में, जो आज [[@bangladesh|बांग्लादेश]] में है, एक मणिपुरी नृत्य देखा। वे इतने भावविभोर हुए कि उन्होंने मणिपुरी गुरुओं को बंगाल में शांतिनिकेतन के अपने विद्यालय में बुला लिया। इससे यह नृत्य बाकी भारत तक पहुँचा, और टैगोर के अपने नृत्य-नाटकों के ज़रिए विदेशी दर्शकों तक भी।

1954 में नए नर्तक तैयार करने के लिए इंफ़ाल में जवाहरलाल [[@nehru|नेहरू]] मणिपुर नृत्य अकादमी खुली। आज मणिपुरी पूरे भारत में सिखाया जाता है और कोलकाता से न्यूयॉर्क तक के मंचों पर होता है।

पोटलोई घाघरा कड़े कपड़े की परतों से बनता है, जिसका निचला हिस्सा इतना सख्त किया जाता है कि वह ढोल की तरह फैला खड़ा रहता है। उस पर [[@mirrors|शीशों]] का काम, सोने-चाँदी के धागे और सितारे लगे होते हैं, जो दीयों की रोशनी में जगमगाते हैं। कृष्ण पीले वस्त्र पहनते हैं और सिर पर मोरपंख का मुकुट। घाघरा पैरों को पूरी तरह ढक लेता है, इसलिए नर्तकियाँ लगभग गुड़ियों की तरह तैरती-सी लगती हैं।

मणिपुर के संगीत में एक गायक, पुंग ढोल, झाँझ और कभी-कभी बाँसुरी होती है। कोमल कदमों के साथ मिलकर यह एक सपने जैसा माहौल बनाता है, और बहुत-से मणिपुरी कहते हैं कि यह नृत्य होना ही ऐसा चाहिए। मणिपुर के लोगों के लिए यह गहरे गर्व की बात भी है, और [[@northeast-india|पूर्वोत्तर भारत]] की सबसे जानी-मानी कलाओं में से एक।

text: Guru Nanak was a spiritual teacher who lived in Punjab from 1469 to 1539. He is the founder of Sikhism and the first of the ten [[@sikh-gurus|Sikh Gurus]]. His name is often written Guru Nanak Dev Ji, as a mark of respect.

He taught that there is one God, present in everyone and everything, and that people come closer to God through honest work, remembering God's name and sharing what they have. He spoke out against empty [[ritual|rituals]] and against treating people as high or low because of their caste.
His hymns, written in Punjabi and related languages, are part of the [[@guru-granth-sahib|Guru Granth Sahib]], the Sikh holy book. Today there are around 2.5 crore Sikhs around the world.

sec.t:
Nanak was born in the village of Talwandi, near Lahore, now called Nankana Sahib in Pakistan. His father, Mehta Kalu, was a village accountant. His older sister, Bebe Nanaki, is remembered as the first person to recognise how special he was.

Stories tell of a thoughtful boy who asked his teachers difficult questions. In one well-known story, his father gave him 20 rupees to make a good business deal. Nanak spent it all feeding hungry holy men, and called it the truest bargain, *sacha sauda*.

As a young man he worked as a storekeeper in the town of Sultanpur Lodhi.

According to Sikh tradition, when Nanak was about 30, he went to bathe in the Kali Bein river and did not come out. Friends feared he had drowned. After three days he returned and said, "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim."

Many understand this to mean that God doesn't see people by religious labels, only by how they live. His teaching opens with the words *Ik Onkar*, "there is one God".

sec.h: A village of farmers and singers
sec.t:
In his later years, Guru Nanak settled at Kartarpur, on the Ravi river, and worked as a farmer. His followers, called Sikhs, meaning learners, lived and worked there too.

They began each day with prayer and sang hymns together in the evening. Everyone ate in a shared kitchen called the langar. Rich and poor, men and women, people of every caste sat on the floor together. The langar continues today in gurdwaras around the world. The one at the [[@golden-temple|Golden Temple]] in Amritsar feeds tens of thousands of people a day.

Before he died in 1539, Guru Nanak chose his follower Lehna, renamed Angad, as the next Guru, rather than either of his sons. His hymns were later gathered by the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, into the [[scripture|scripture]] completed in 1604.

Guru Nanak's birthday, Gurpurab, is celebrated on the full moon of the month of Kartik, in October or November. Gurdwaras are lit up, hymns are sung through the night, and processions fill the streets.

Kartarpur is now in Pakistan, just a few kilometres from the border with India. In 2019, for the 550th anniversary of his birth, the two countries opened the Kartarpur Corridor so pilgrims from India could visit without a visa.

text: People move from villages to cities mostly for work. Farming depends on rain and land, and a small family farm often cannot feed or employ everyone. Cities offer jobs in building sites, factories, shops, offices and homes, and they usually pay more.

Other reasons pull people too: better colleges, hospitals, or the chance to join relatives who have already moved. Experts call these "push" and "pull" factors. A bad harvest or debt pushes someone out of a village. A cousin with a job in Surat pulls them in. Often both happen at once.
India's 2011 Census counted about 45.6 crore internal migrants, people living somewhere other than the place they used to live. That was more than one in three Indians.

sec.h: Not always the journey you'd expect
sec.t:
The picture of a young man boarding a train to Mumbai is real, but it is only part of the story. Most migration in India happens within the same state. A large share is from village to village.

The biggest single reason for women is marriage, because many brides move to their husband's home. For men, work comes first. Some families [[migration|migrate]] for a season, going to work in brick [[kiln|kilns]] or sugarcane fields for a few months and returning home for the rest of the year.

Long-distance moves often follow well-worn paths, from states like Uttar Pradesh and Bihar to big cities like Delhi and Mumbai. The [[@indian-railways|railways]] carry many of these journeys, and some long-distance trains are packed with migrant workers around festivals.

{{story:indian-railways}}

Many migrants send part of their earnings back to their village. This money pays for school fees, medicines, a new roof or a well. Whole villages can change because of what relatives earn hundreds of kilometres away. In parts of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha, money from city jobs is a big part of what keeps many households going. Migrants also carry ideas home: new recipes, new words, new ways of doing things.

City life is often hard at first. Rent is high, so many newcomers share small rooms or live in [[@slums-housing|slums]]. Many work without contracts, so they can lose their jobs without warning.

That became painfully clear in 2020. When India went into its first COVID-19 lockdown, factories and building sites shut. With trains stopped, many thousands of migrant workers set out to walk or cycle home, some across several states. Special trains and buses were later arranged. The sight of families walking along highways made many people notice how much their cities depend on workers from far away.

The USA saw its own huge move. From the 1910s to 1970, about six million African Americans left the farms of the rural South for cities in the North and West, such as Chicago, Detroit and New York. They were escaping unfair laws, violence and poor pay, and seeking factory jobs.

Their move changed the country. It helped create the [[@harlem-renaissance|Harlem Renaissance]] in New York, spread jazz and [[@blues|blues]], and built the strength of the [[@civil-rights|civil rights]] movement.

Around 2007, according to the United Nations, more than half the people on Earth were living in towns and cities for the first time. India is still more rural than most: in 2011, only about 31% of Indians lived in urban areas. That share is growing, and planners expect India's cities to keep swelling for decades. Some villages are themselves turning into towns, as shops, colleges and roads arrive. The line between village and city is getting blurrier every year.

text: A trade union is a group of workers who join together to deal with their employer as one. One worker asking for better pay or safer machines can easily be ignored or fired. Hundreds asking together are much harder to ignore.

Unions bargain with employers over pay, working hours, holidays and safety. This is called collective bargaining. If talks fail, union members may go on strike, which means they stop working until a deal is reached. Unions also help members who are treated unfairly, and many campaign for laws that protect all workers, union members or not.

sec.t:
Unions grew up alongside factories. During the [[@industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]], workers often laboured 12 to 16 hours a day, six days a week, in dangerous mills. Children worked beside adults. Employers held almost all the power.

In many countries, joining a union was at first treated as a crime. In 1834, six farm workers from the village of Tolpuddle in England were sentenced to be sent to Australia for forming a union. Huge protests followed, and they were later pardoned. Over the following decades, most industrial countries made unions legal.

sec.h: May Day and the eight-hour day
sec.t:
In the USA, the American Federation of Labor was founded in 1886. That year, on 1 May, hundreds of thousands of American workers went on strike for an eight-hour working day. In [[@chicago|Chicago]], a protest in Haymarket Square days later ended with a bomb and deaths.

The campaign spread worldwide, and 1 May became Workers' Day in many countries. In America, workers are honoured instead on Labor Day, the first Monday in September.

A disaster in New York pushed the movement further. In 1911, a fire broke out at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory, where many of the workers were young immigrant women. Some exit doors were locked, and 146 people died. The tragedy led to new fire safety laws, and the garment workers' union grew much stronger.

{{story:chicago}}

India's [[@textiles-india|textile mills]] were the birthplace of its labour movement. In 1890, N. M. Lokhande formed the Bombay Mill Hands Association. In 1918, workers in [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]]'s mills struck for higher wages. [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] supported them and went on a fast, one of his first, and the mill owners agreed to arbitration.

Anasuya Sarabhai, the sister of one of the mill owners, sided with the workers. She helped form the Textile Labour Association in 1920. The same year, the All India Trade Union Congress was founded in Bombay, with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president. The Trade Unions Act of 1926 allowed unions to register legally.

Supporters say unions give ordinary workers a fair voice and helped build the middle class in many countries. Workers in unions often earn more and have better benefits.

Critics argue that strikes can shut down hospitals, trains or schools and hurt the public. Some say high union wages can make companies less competitive or slow to change. In the USA, about one wage worker in ten belonged to a union in 2024, far fewer than in the 1950s. In India, most workers are in the informal sector, without a regular employer, which makes organising harder. New groups, like unions for delivery riders, are now trying to change that.

text: A whole number is even if you can split it into pairs with nothing left over, and odd if one is always left alone. Six socks make three pairs, so 6 is even. Seven socks leave one lonely sock, so 7 is odd. In maths language, even numbers can be divided by 2 exactly, and odd ones leave a remainder of 1.

Even and odd numbers take turns along the number line: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, odd, even, odd, even, odd. That simple pattern turns out to be useful in places you might not expect, from computer memory to [[@road-safety|traffic rules]] and the way houses are numbered on a street.

sec.t:
To tell if a big number is even, you only need to look at its last digit. If it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, it is even. If it ends in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9, it is odd. So 4,58,93,276 is even, however long it is.

This works because every 10 is even. Any big number is a lot of tens plus its last digit. The tens can always be paired up, so only the last digit can leave one over. The same idea means 2 is the only even [[@prime-numbers|prime number]], since every other even number divides by 2.

Even and odd numbers follow neat rules when you add them. Even plus even is even. Odd plus odd is even, because the two leftovers pair up with each other. Even plus odd is odd. Multiplying is simpler still: the answer is odd only if both numbers are odd.

These rules can save time. If someone adds 15 odd numbers and claims the total is 100, you know they made a mistake, because an odd count of odd numbers always gives an odd total.

[[@maths-games|Board games]] make use of them too. On an ordinary six-sided die, opposite faces add up to 7. So every odd face sits opposite an even one: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4.

{{story:board-games}}

sec.h: Odd and even on the road
sec.t:
In January 2016, the city of [[@delhi|Delhi]] tried an unusual experiment to fight [[@air-pollution|air pollution]]. On odd dates, only private cars with number plates ending in an odd digit could drive. On even dates, only those ending in an even digit. There were exceptions for emergency vehicles, women driving alone and some others. The rule has been brought back several times since, usually in winter. Scientists still disagree about how much it cleaned the air. Cities such as Paris and [[@mexico|Mexico]] City have tried similar schemes.

Many streets in India, the United States and Britain number houses with odd numbers on one side and even numbers on the other. That way, a [[@people-postman-village|postman]] knows which side to walk along.

sec.h: Even and odd in daily life
sec.t:
In computers, a trick called a parity check uses even and odd to catch errors. When a computer sends a block of [[@binary-code|binary]] digits, it can add one extra bit to make the number of 1s even. If a block arrives with an odd number of 1s, the computer knows something got scrambled along the way.

Some customs care about odd numbers too. At many Indian [[@weddings-india|weddings]] and festivals, people give gifts of money such as 101, 501 or 1,001 rupees. Many families say the extra one rupee is a blessing, a sign that the giving should continue and not end in a round, finished number.

Add the odd numbers in order and watch. 1 = 1, 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16. Every total is a square number. Draw it with dots and you will see why. Each new odd number wraps neatly around two sides of the square before, making it one row and one column bigger.

text: Start with simple maths. If a recipe feeds 4 and you need to feed 100, divide 100 by 4. That gives a scale factor of 25. Multiply every ingredient by 25, so 2 cups of rice becomes 50 cups and 1 onion becomes 25.

That gets you close, and for many dishes it is enough. But big cooks know three traps. Strong flavours like salt and chilli can overpower a big pot, so they are added slowly and tasted. Big pots and tins heat in strange ways, because of how area and volume grow. And a kitchen needs equipment that is big enough. Scaling a recipe is really two jobs: maths for the shopping list and cooking sense for everything else.

st.prompt: Your recipe uses a round cake tin 20 cm across. You want to bake in a 40 cm tin, same depth. How much more batter do you need?

options.t: 2 times as much
4 times as much
8 times as much

st.reveal: The tin is twice as wide in two directions, across and along, so its floor has 2 × 2 = 4 times the area. At the same depth, that means four times the batter. If the cake were twice as deep as well, you would need eight times as much.

src: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, Langar at Sri Harmandir Sahib.

McGee H., On Food and Cooking (Scribner, 2004).

myth: To feed ten times as many people, you just multiply every ingredient and cooking time by ten.

sec.h: The kitchen that feeds a city
sec.t:
At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the free kitchen, or langar, often serves 50,000 or more people a day, and well over a lakh on festival days. Volunteers sit in rows rolling rotis, and machines can turn out thousands an hour.

Nobody there multiplies a family recipe by 25,000. Langar cooks work from experience, in units of whole sacks of flour and giant cauldrons, called *degs*, that can each hold enough dal for thousands. They taste, adjust and taste again.

{{story:golden-temple}}

India's school lunch scheme is even bigger. Under PM POSHAN, the [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]] programme, more than ten crore children are given lunch on school days. Some central kitchens cook more than a lakh meals before the bell rings for lunch.

Here is the trick that catches people out. Take a square tin 20 cm on each side. Double the side to 40 cm and the floor of the tin is 2 × 2 = 4 times bigger. Keep the batter the same depth, and you need four times as much.

Now double a ball of dough in every direction. It grows 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times in volume. This is the square-cube rule, and it explains why big things behave differently from small ones. A giant cake has much more inside compared with its surface. Heat comes in through the surface, so the middle cooks last. Big bakers often lower the oven temperature and bake for longer, so the outside doesn't burn while the centre is still gooey. The same rule explains why an elephant needs thick legs, and why [[@area-volume|area and volume]] puzzles show up everywhere.

sec.h: Salt, spice and the taste test
sec.t:
Cooks often say: scale the rice, scale the vegetables, but go slowly on salt and spice. In a huge pot, less liquid boils away for each litre of food, so flavours don't concentrate as much. Some spices also seem to get stronger in large batches.

The safe method is to add about three quarters of the full amount, taste, then add more if needed. You can always add salt. You can't take it out.

Scaling down is a maths puzzle too. Halving a recipe that uses 3 eggs gives you one and a half. Cooks either beat 2 eggs and use three quarters, or round up and accept a slightly richer cake. Turning 2⅔ cups into a recipe for one person means dividing [[@fractions|fractions]], which is good practice for a test, and even better practice for dessert.

At an Indian wedding, a *halwai* might cook for 500 guests over two days. In the USA, a Thanksgiving dinner for 20 means a turkey that needs hours in the oven. In both kitchens the rule is the same: write the scaled list down, buy a little extra and taste constantly. The best large-scale cooks treat recipes as a [[@ratios-cooking|ratio]], not a list of fixed amounts, which is exactly how a cup of chai stays the same whether you make one or fifty.

text: Snowflakes have six sides because of the shape of water itself. A water [[molecule|molecule]] is made of one oxygen [[atom|atom]] and two hydrogen atoms, joined in a bent shape like a wide "V". When water freezes, those molecules link up in a pattern of rings, and each ring has six sides.

So every ice crystal begins as a tiny hexagon. As it falls through a cloud, water vapour freezes onto its six corners, which stick out the most. The corners grow into arms. Because all six arms grow in the same air at the same time, they usually end up looking alike. That gives a snowflake its six-fold [[@symmetry|symmetry]].

st.prompt: Scientists can grow snowflakes in a lab. At about −5 °C, what shape do the ice crystals usually take?

options.t: Thin needles and columns
Big feathery stars
Perfect round balls

st.reveal: Shape depends on temperature and how damp the air is. Around −5 °C, crystals grow as needles and columns. The big feathery stars grow best near −15 °C in very moist air.

src: Kenneth Libbrecht, Caltech, SnowCrystals.com and The Snowflake - Winter's Secret Beauty (2003).
Johannes Kepler, The Six-Cornered Snowflake (1611).

d.try: Fold a square of paper in half, then fold it into three equal wedges so you get a narrow triangle. Snip small shapes out of the edges with safety scissors and unfold it. You will get a six-sided pattern, because each cut is copied six times, just like a snowflake's arms.
myth: Every snowflake is a perfect six-pointed star.
Most snowflakes are lumpy, broken or stuck together in clumps. The neat stars form only in certain conditions. But underneath, the ice in every one is arranged in a six-sided pattern.

Biggest star-shaped flakes grow at about −15 °C

sec.t:
In 1611, the German [[astronomer|astronomer]] Johannes Kepler wanted to give his friend a New Year's gift. He was short of money, so he wrote a little book instead. It asked why snowflakes always have six corners.

Kepler had no [[microscope|microscope]] strong enough to see molecules. He guessed the answer might lie in how tiny round pieces pack together, like cannonballs stacked on a ship. He was on the right track. It took about 300 years, and X-ray machines, for scientists to see the six-sided arrangement of molecules inside ice.

People often think the arms somehow copy each other. They don't. A snowflake is so small, about the width of a pencil eraser, that all its arms meet the same temperature and dampness as it tumbles. When the air gets colder, all six arms change their growth together. When it gets damper, all six sprout side branches together.

So a snowflake's shape is a record of its trip through the cloud. Two flakes take different paths, so they look different. With billions of molecules in each flake and countless possible paths, finding two exactly alike is almost impossible.

In the 1930s, the Japanese scientist Ukichiro Nakaya became the first to grow snowflakes in a lab. He found that temperature and dampness decide the shape. Near −2 °C, crystals form flat plates. Near −5 °C, they grow as needles and columns. Near −15 °C, in very moist air, they become the large, branching stars we draw on cards.

So skiers in Gulmarg and children in Buffalo, New York, may see totally different snow on the same day. Nakaya called snowflakes "letters from the sky", because their shape tells you about the clouds they came from. Snowflakes drift down slowly, at roughly walking pace, which gives them time to grow on the way. And although each crystal is clear ice, snow looks white because its countless tiny faces scatter every colour of light.

Six-sided shapes turn up all over nature. [[basalt|Basalt]] rock can crack into hexagonal columns. Bees build their honey stores from six-sided wax cells. Mathematicians have even invented a snowflake that never ends: each side keeps sprouting smaller bumps forever, a kind of [[@fractals|fractal]] shape. And the strangest part? Bees chose the hexagon for a completely different reason than ice did, as the story of the [[@honeycomb|honeycomb]] shows.

text: The Paralympics are the world's biggest sporting event for athletes with disabilities. They are held every four years, soon after the Summer and Winter [[@olympics|Olympics]], in the same city and venues. Athletes compete in sports from [[@swimming|swimming]] and athletics to wheelchair [[@basketball|basketball]] and blind football.

The name comes from the Greek word "para", meaning beside or alongside. The Games stand side by side with the Olympics. At the Paris 2024 Paralympics, about 4,400 athletes from more than 160 teams took part.

st.prompt: In goalball, a Paralympic sport for blind and partially sighted players, how do players know where the ball is?

options.t: The ball has bells inside it
A coach shouts directions
The ball glows brightly

st.reveal: Goalball players wear blackout eyeshades so everyone competes equally, and they track the ball by the sound of bells inside it. Spectators must stay silent during play.

d.try: With an adult's help, try a sound game. One person rolls a ball with a small bell, or a plastic bottle with rice in it, gently across the floor. The other, with eyes closed, tries to stop it by listening. Notice how much harder you have to concentrate.
myth: The Paralympics and the Special Olympics are the same thing.

They are separate. The Paralympics are elite competitions for athletes with a range of physical, visual and some intellectual impairments. The Special Olympics are for people with intellectual disabilities and focus on taking part at every level.

sec.h: A doctor and a hospital lawn
sec.t:
The story begins with Dr Ludwig Guttmann, a Jewish doctor who fled Nazi Germany in 1939 and settled in England. During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], he ran a unit for people with spinal cord injuries at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, north-west of London.

At the time, most patients with such injuries were expected to stay in bed and many died young. Guttmann believed sport could help them get stronger and feel hopeful. On 29 July 1948, the same day the London Olympics opened, he held an archery competition for 16 wheelchair users, most of them injured ex-servicemen and women. He called it the Stoke Mandeville Games.

sec.h: From hospital games to world stage

sec.t:
Paralympic sport uses a system called classification. Athletes are grouped with others whose impairment affects their sport in a similar way. A swimmer with one arm will race others with similar limits, not someone with a visual impairment.

Some sports exist only at the Paralympics. Goalball, for blind and partially sighted players, uses a ball with bells inside. In boccia, athletes with severe impairments throw or roll leather balls towards a target ball, sometimes using a ramp. Technology helps too. Carbon-fibre running blades and light sports wheelchairs are designed with the help of engineers and [[@sports-science|sports scientists]].

[[@sport-paralympians-india|India's first Paralympic gold]] came in 1972, when Murlikant Petkar won the 50 metres freestyle swim in Germany, setting a world record. He was a soldier who had been badly wounded in the 1965 war.

Javelin thrower Devendra Jhajharia won gold in 2004 and 2016. High jumper Mariyappan Thangavelu won gold in Rio. At Tokyo, [[@shooting-sport|shooter]] Avani Lekhara became the first Indian woman to win a Paralympic gold, and she won again in Paris. India won 19 medals at Tokyo and 29 in Paris, far more than at its [[@olympics-india|Olympic]] appearances.

The Paralympic symbol is three curved shapes in red, blue and green, called agitos, from a Latin word meaning "I move". The motto is "Spirit in Motion".

Guttmann hoped the Games would change how people saw disability, and over the decades crowds and television audiences have grown. At London 2012 the stadium was full night after night. Away from sport, inventions such as [[@braille|braille]] have opened up reading and work in the same spirit. The Paralympics showed millions that a wheelchair or a missing limb is not the end of a sporting dream.

text: A Test match can last up to five days because each team gets two innings. To win, you must get all 20 of the other side's batters out while scoring more runs. Good batters can bat for hours, so taking 20 wickets takes a long time.

Each day has about 90 overs, split into three sessions with breaks for lunch and tea. If one team wins quickly, the match ends early. If time runs out before a result, it is a draw, which makes Tests very different from shorter formats where someone always wins.

st.prompt: In 1939 a "timeless Test" in Durban, South Africa, was meant to go on until there was a result. How did it end?

options.t: As a draw, because England had to leave to catch their ship home
England won on the 12th day
Rain washed out the final week

st.reveal: The match lasted 10 days of play spread across 12 days. England needed just 42 more runs with five wickets left, but their ship was leaving. The match was declared a draw, and no timeless Test has been played since.

d.try: Watch a short highlights video of a Test match pitch on day 1 and on day 5, with an adult's help. Look for cracks, dusty patches and footmarks. Then think about how each change would help a fast bowler or a spinner.
myth: If a Test match lasts all five days, somebody must win.
Many Tests end in a draw. To win, a team must bowl the other side out twice and score more runs. If time runs out before that, nobody wins, even if one team is far ahead.

sec.t:
Cricket has been played with two innings per side since its early days in England. Two innings give a team a chance to recover from a bad start, and they make the match a long test of skill, patience and fitness.

That is where the name comes from. Matches between national sides came to be called "Test" matches because they were seen as the toughest test of each country's strength. The first was played at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in [[@australia|Australia]] in March 1877. Australia beat England by 45 runs.

Draws can be exciting. A team far behind may bat for a whole day to "save" the match. Rain often plays a part too, which is why fans check the [[@chance-weather|weather forecast]] as nervously as the scorecard.

A tie, where both sides finish with exactly the same score after all four innings, is much rarer. It has happened only twice in nearly 150 years, in Brisbane in 1960 and in Madras (now [[@chennai|Chennai]]) in 1986, when India played Australia.

Some early Tests had no time limit at all. The most famous, in Durban in 1939, lasted 12 days and still ended in a draw.

India played its first Test at Lord's in London in 1932, captained by C. K. Nayudu. India lost, but its fast bowler Mohammad Nissar impressed the English crowd. India's first Test win came in 1952, against England in Madras.

India has since produced great Test players, from Sunil Gavaskar and Kapil Dev to [[@sachin-tendulkar|Sachin Tendulkar]], who played 200 Tests.

Players in Tests traditionally wear white and use a red ball. Since 2015, some Tests have been played at night under floodlights, with a pink ball that is easier to see in the dark. The World Test Championship, started in 2019, gives Test series a league table and a final.

Twelve countries have full Test status. Many worry that shorter, richer formats like the [[@ipl|IPL]] leave less room for Tests. Yet the five-day game survives because it is the one format where a team can be losing badly on day two and still win on day five.

text: Nobody invented fire. It was already there, in grass fires lit by [[@lightning|lightning]] and in smouldering logs after a storm. Early humans first learned to use it: carrying a burning branch, feeding it with wood and keeping it alive. Much later, they learned to start a fire whenever they wanted.

The evidence comes from charcoal, ash, burnt bones and stones changed by heat, found in [[@caves-form|caves]] and old campsites. The oldest strong clues are about a million years old, from a cave in [[@south-africa|South Africa]]. By around 400,000 years ago, fire shows up at many sites in Africa, Europe and Asia.

st.prompt: Roughly how old is some of the oldest strong evidence of people controlling fire?

options.t: About 1 million years
About 10,000 years, when farming began
About 5,000 years, in ancient Egypt

st.reveal: Ash and burnt bones from Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa are about a million years old. That is long before our own species existed. By about 400,000 years ago, fire was used regularly in many places.

src: Berna F. et al. (2012) Microstratigraphic evidence of in situ fire in the Acheulean strata of Wonderwerk Cave. PNAS 109.

n.certNote: Burnt bones and ash are hard to read. Scientists argue about when fire was first controlled, how often early humans used it, and when they could start one from scratch.

d.try: Rub your palms together fast for ten seconds and feel how warm they get. Now try it slowly. That heat comes from friction, the same effect people used to light fires by spinning a stick against wood. Only an adult should ever try real fire-making, and only outdoors.
myth: Fire was discovered in one moment by one clever person.

Early humans probably used fire from wildfires and lightning for a very long time before they could start one themselves. Learning to control and make fire likely happened slowly, and in more than one place.

sec.t:
Finding ancient fire is tricky. A wildfire can scorch bones and soil too. So scientists look for signs that a fire burned in one spot, again and again, inside a shelter where lightning could not reach.

At Wonderwerk Cave, researchers found fine ash and burnt bone fragments about 30 metres inside the cave, layered as if from small fires. At Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel, burnt seeds, wood and flint about 790,000 years old cluster in patches, like old hearths. Some claims of even older fires exist, but many scientists are not convinced.

Fire kept people warm and let them live in colder lands. It scared away animals at night. Its light stretched the day, giving hours for talking, making tools and telling stories.

It also changed food. [[@cooking-science|Cooking]] softens meat and roots, kills many germs and makes food easier to digest. The scientist Richard Wrangham has argued that cooking gave early humans so much extra energy that it helped their brains grow larger. Others think brains began growing before regular fire use, so the idea is still debated.

People also used fire as a tool. They hardened the tips of wooden spears, and in South Africa, at least 160,000 years ago, people heated stone to make it easier to chip into sharp blades.

Because fire mattered so much, many cultures tell stories about it. In [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]], Prometheus steals fire from the gods and gives it to humans. Many [[@myths-native-american|Native American stories]] tell of an animal, such as a spider or a coyote, carrying fire to people.

In India, fire is sacred in Hindu worship. The very first hymn of the Rigveda, one of the oldest texts in any Indian language, praises Agni, the god of fire. Today, fire still sits at the centre of Hindu weddings, Parsi fire temples and the oil lamps of [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]].

For most of history, starting a fire was slow work, so people kept embers glowing or borrowed fire from neighbours. [[@made-matchsticks|Friction matches]] were invented in England in 1826. Safety matches, which light only when struck on the box, followed in Sweden in the 1840s and 1850s. A trick that once took minutes of hard work now takes one flick of the wrist.

text: In 1893 a 23-year-old lawyer named Mohandas Gandhi sailed to Durban to help an Indian trading firm with a court case. He meant to stay a year. Instead, he spent 21 years in South Africa, which was then made up of British colonies and settler states.

There, Indians were treated as second-class people by law. Gandhi set up organisations, ran a newspaper, and went to jail several times. Most important, he developed *satyagraha*, a way of resisting injustice without violence. When he returned to India in 1915, he was already famous, and ready to use the same method against British rule.

st.prompt: In 1893, why was Gandhi pushed off a train at Pietermaritzburg station?

A white passenger objected to an Indian sitting in first class
He was travelling to the wrong city

st.reveal: Gandhi had a first-class ticket. A white passenger complained, and when Gandhi refused to move to a lower class, a police constable pushed him off. He spent a cold night in the waiting room, thinking about whether to stay and fight or go home.

d.try: Gandhi kept a newspaper going for over a decade to spread ideas. Make a one-page class newspaper with three short stories about something unfair you'd like to change at school, such as too little shade in the playground. Share it and count how many people agree.
myth: Gandhi went to South Africa as a political leader to help Indians there.
He went as a young, little-known lawyer hired to help with one business case. He became a leader only after he saw how Indians were treated and decided to stay and organise.

sec.t:
About two weeks after arriving, Gandhi took a train from Durban towards Pretoria with a first-class ticket. At Pietermaritzburg station, a white passenger objected to sharing the compartment with an Indian. Gandhi refused to move to the van compartment. He was pushed off the train and his luggage was thrown after him.

He sat all night in the freezing waiting room. Later he wrote that this was when he decided to stay and fight the "deep disease of colour prejudice". Today a plaque at the station marks the spot.

sec.h: Why Indians were in South Africa

sec.t:
In 1906 the Transvaal government ordered every Indian to register and carry a pass with fingerprints. On 11 September, about 3,000 Indians packed a theatre in Johannesburg and swore they would not obey, whatever the punishment.

Gandhi called this new method [[satyagraha|satyagraha]], from Sanskrit words meaning "holding on to truth". The idea was to refuse unfair laws openly, accept punishment calmly, and never hit back. Over the next years, thousands of Indians went to jail.

sec.h: Farms, a newspaper and a long march
sec.t:
Gandhi started a newspaper, *Indian Opinion*, in 1903. He set up two communal farms, Phoenix Settlement near Durban and Tolstoy Farm near Johannesburg, where families grew food and shared work. Gandhi learned to bake bread and make sandals there.

In 1913, the movement reached its peak. Thousands of Indian mine workers went on strike and marched across the border from Natal into the Transvaal, breaking the law on purpose. Gandhi's wife, Kasturba, was jailed too. The next year the government agreed to scrap the three-pound tax and recognise Indian marriages.

Gandhi's struggle in South Africa was for Indians, not for the Black African majority, who suffered even worse treatment. His early writings include insulting remarks about Black Africans. Some people say his views widened later in life. Others say these remarks should not be brushed aside. In 2018, a statue of him was removed from a university campus in Ghana after protests.

Many Black South African leaders still drew on his ideas. [[@nelson-mandela|Nelson Mandela]] called Gandhi an inspiration, and both South Africa and India claim him as part of their story.

text: The people of the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]], such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, used a set of signs between about 2600 and 1900 BCE. They carved them on small square seals, pots, copper tablets and bangles. More than 4,000 inscribed objects have been found.

The trouble is that the texts are tiny. Most have about five signs, and none is long. Nobody knows what language the Indus people spoke, and no [[inscription|inscription]] has turned up that gives the same words in a known script. Without a long text, a known language or a translation, there is very little to grab hold of.

st.prompt: Egyptian hieroglyphs were cracked thanks to a stone with the same text in three scripts. Has anything like that turned up for the Indus script?

options.t: No, no such two-language inscription has ever been found
Yes, but it is too damaged to read
Yes, and it was translated in 2004

st.reveal: No bilingual text has ever been found. The Rosetta Stone let scholars match Egyptian signs to Greek words they already knew. Without a key like that, Indus signs can only be studied by spotting patterns.

src.Iravatham Mahadevan, The Indus Script: Texts, Concordance and Tables (Archaeological Survey of India, 1977).

src: Asko Parpola, Deciphering the Indus Script (Cambridge University Press, 1994).
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Indus script.
n.certNote: Most experts think the signs record a language, but a few argue they are symbols that never wrote down speech. Nobody knows which language it would be, and every claimed decipherment so far has been rejected by other scholars.

d.try: Invent your own five-sign script. Draw a small picture for each of five words, write a short message on a slip of paper and give it to a friend without explaining anything. See how much they can work out from patterns alone, then swap.
myth: The Indus script was deciphered years ago.
Many people have announced a decipherment, some in newspapers. None has convinced other experts, because none can read new inscriptions in a way that others can test and repeat.

sec.t:
A typical Indus seal is about the size of a postage stamp, carved from a soft stone called steatite. Many show an animal, often a one-horned creature that looks like a [[@myths-unicorns|unicorn]], with a row of signs above it.

Traders probably pressed the seals into wet clay to mark bundles of goods, a bit like a stamp on a parcel today. That would explain why the messages are so short. A name, a title or the owner's town needs only a few signs. In 1875, the British [[archaeologist|archaeologist]] Alexander Cunningham published one of these seals from Harappa. He had no idea that it belonged to a [[civilisation|civilisation]] thousands of years older than he guessed.

In 2004 three researchers argued that the signs were not writing at all. They said the signs might be symbols, like road signs or family badges, that never recorded spoken words.

Other scientists answered by studying how often each sign follows another. They found patterns that look much more like language than like random symbols. The argument has not been settled. There is also no agreement on the language. Some scholars, including Mahadevan and the Finnish expert Asko Parpola, think it was an early form of a Dravidian language, related to Tamil. Others prefer links to Sanskrit or to a language that has since vanished.

At Dholavira, in the [[@gujarat-rann|Rann of Kutch]] in Gujarat, archaeologists in the early 1990s found ten large signs lying on the ground near a gateway. Each sign is roughly as tall as a school ruler is long. They may once have been fixed to a wooden board above the gate, like a city's name over its entrance.

Even this, the biggest Indus inscription, is only ten signs. It shows that the script was used in public as well as on seals, and that ordinary passers-by may once have read it easily.

Code-breakers need more text. A long inscription, or a bilingual one, could change everything. Indus seals have been found as far away as [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], so a seal with a matching cuneiform label is one hope. Until then, the script remains one of the great unsolved puzzles of the ancient world, sitting on museum shelves in Delhi, Karachi and London.

text: People have gathered to ride, play and eat at fairs and pleasure gardens for hundreds of years. Bakken in Denmark has welcomed visitors since 1583, and Tivoli Gardens in Copenhagen opened in 1843. By 1900, New York's Coney Island had roller coasters and bright electric lights.

What changed in 1955 was the idea of a *theme*. Walt Disney, a cartoon maker, opened Disneyland in Anaheim, California, on 17 July that year. Instead of a jumble of rides, each area told a story: a small-town main street, a jungle river, a castle from a fairy tale. That idea now shapes parks from Florida to Shanghai.

st.prompt: Disneyland's first day in 1955 had many problems. Which of these really happened?

options.t: Freshly laid asphalt was so soft in the heat that shoes sank into it
The castle collapsed
No visitors came

st.reveal: It was a scorching July day, and new asphalt on Main Street turned soft and sticky. Far more people arrived than expected, some with fake tickets, and food ran out. The park got better fast, and within about two months it had welcomed its millionth visitor.

myth: Walt Disney invented the amusement park.
Amusement parks with rides and games are centuries older. Disney's new idea was a "theme park", where every part of the park tells a story and visitors can't see the outside world from inside.

sec.t:
The old pleasure gardens of Europe were green parks with music, lamps, dancing and food stalls. Fairs added swings and wooden carousels, turned first by horses or people and later by steam engines. In the 1890s, Coney Island at the edge of New York City became the place where working families went for a cheap day out. They rode early roller coasters, watched shows and stared at buildings covered in thousands of light bulbs.

The story goes that Walt Disney had the idea for his own park while sitting on a bench, watching his two daughters ride a merry-go-round. He thought parents deserved somewhere they could enjoy too, cleaner and better planned than the fairs he knew. He spent years sketching ideas, and even built a small steam railway in his own garden.

sec.h: A park built like a film set

sec.t:
The first day was chaotic. Tens of thousands of people turned up, many with forged tickets. The July heat softened fresh asphalt, there weren't enough drinking fountains, and some rides broke down. Newspapers were not kind.

Disney fixed the problems quickly. Within about two months the park had welcomed its millionth guest, and families were driving across the country to see it. It helped that Disney had a weekly TV show, so children in faraway states already knew the park before they arrived.

Walt Disney World opened near Orlando, Florida, in 1971, on land so large it could hold a city. Its Magic Kingdom park drew about 1.8 crore visitors in 2024, more than any other theme park on Earth. Disneyland in California came second.

Parks followed in Tokyo (1983), near Paris (1992), Hong Kong (2005) and Shanghai (2016). As of 2025, Disney runs 12 parks at six resorts. [[@tokyo|Tokyo]] has two of them side by side.

Theme parks sell a safe kind of fright. A drop ride lets you fall for a second or two, long enough for [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] to make your stomach lurch but never long enough to be dangerous. Engineers test every ride with sandbags and dummies before people climb aboard.

India has its own big parks, such as EsselWorld near Mumbai, which opened in 1989, and the Wonderla parks in cities such as Kochi, Bengaluru and Hyderabad. Most mix water slides with roller coasters, which suits a hot [[climate|climate]]. The [[@neuschwanstein|fairy-tale castle]], though, still belongs to a mouse born in a 1928 cartoon.

text: Chand Baori is about 30 metres deep, roughly as tall as a 10-storey building. It drops through 13 levels of stairs to a pool of water at the bottom. Its walls are lined with around 3,500 narrow steps, arranged in criss-crossing flights that make a pattern of sharp triangles.

It stands in Abhaneri, a village about 95 km east of [[@jaipur|Jaipur]]. It is one of India's oldest and deepest [[@stepwells|stepwells]]. Most historians date it to the 8th or 9th century, when a local ruler called Raja Chanda is said to have built it. People came here for water, for shade and to pray at the temple next door.

st.prompt: Why did people build Chand Baori so deep?

options.t: To reach water that sank far underground in the dry months
To hide treasure from invading armies
To store grain where rats could not reach it

st.reveal: In Rajasthan, the water table can drop by many metres between monsoons. A deep well with steps lets people follow the water down as it sinks, all year round.

n.certNote: Chand Baori is usually dated to the 8th or 9th century and linked to a local king called Chanda, but there are few written records. The step count and depth are commonly quoted round figures.

This is a popular local legend. In fact it was built by skilled masons over a long time, and later rulers added the arched pavilions on one side.

sec.t:
Rajasthan gets most of its rain in a few [[monsoon|monsoon]] weeks. After that, the sky can stay dry for eight months. The [[@groundwater|groundwater]] that soaks into the soil then sinks lower and lower.

A normal well needs a long rope and a bucket. A stepwell lets people walk down to the water itself, wherever it happens to be. In August the water might be high up the steps. By May you might have to climb down 10 storeys to fill your pot. The criss-cross stairs let many people go up and down at once without bumping into each other.

The builders also had to stop the walls caving in. Loose soil pushes inwards with huge force at 30 metres down. So the sides of Chand Baori slope gently inwards as they go deeper, making the pit narrower at the bottom than at the top. The square shape and the stepped walls work like a giant set of braces, holding back the earth on every side. It has stood for well over a thousand years.

sec.h: A cool room in the desert

sec.t:
From above, the steps look like a giant puzzle. Each flight forms a small triangle, and the triangles repeat across three walls like a [[@tessellations|tessellation]]. Your eyes keep trying to count them and losing track.

That look has made Chand Baori famous with filmmakers. It appeared in the fantasy film *The Fall* in 2006, and in the Batman film *The Dark Knight Rises* in 2012 as a prison in a deep pit.

Right beside the baori stands the Harshat Mata temple, dedicated to a goddess of joy. It was built around the same time but was badly damaged hundreds of years ago. Broken carvings from it now sit around the walls of the baori, including dancers and musicians.

Many people would wash at the stepwell before going into the temple. Water and worship were tied together in places like this.

The water at the bottom is now green and still, and visitors are no longer allowed down the steps. You watch from a railing at the top. Every year, the village holds the Abhaneri Festival, with folk dancers, puppet shows and camel rides.

Chand Baori is deep, but it is not the most decorated. About 600 km away in Gujarat, the [[@india-wonder-rani-ki-vav|Rani ki Vav]] is covered with hundreds of carved gods and goddesses, so beautiful that it appears on India's 100-rupee note.

text: Kannada and Telugu are both well over a thousand years old as written languages, and the spoken languages are older still. The oldest known Kannada [[inscription|inscription]], the Halmidi stone in Karnataka, is usually dated to about 450 CE, though some experts think it is a little later. The earliest Telugu inscriptions come from around 575 CE.

Both belong to the Dravidian family of languages, alongside [[@tamil-ancient|Tamil]] and [[@malayalam|Malayalam]]. Today about 8 crore people speak Telugu and over 4 crore speak Kannada as their first language, according to the 2011 Census. In 2008, the Government of India declared both to be classical languages, a title for languages with a long, rich and independent history.

st.prompt: Kannada and Telugu are spoken in South India. Which language family do they belong to?

options.t: The Dravidian family, with Tamil and Malayalam
The same family as Sanskrit and Hindi
They have no family; each is completely alone

st.reveal: Kannada and Telugu are Dravidian languages, related to Tamil and Malayalam. They borrowed many words from Sanskrit over the centuries, but their grammar and core words come from a different family tree.

myth: All the languages of South India come from Sanskrit.
Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Malayalam belong to the Dravidian family, which is separate from Sanskrit's family. They borrowed many Sanskrit words, but their roots and grammar are their own.

sec.t:
Linguists think the Dravidian languages grew from one shared ancestor, often called Proto-Dravidian, spoken thousands of years ago. Over many centuries, groups of speakers drifted apart and their speech changed in different ways, until they became separate languages.

Kannada and Telugu still share many words. "Water" is *neeru* in Kannada and *neellu* in Telugu. Both also borrowed heavily from Sanskrit, especially for religious, scientific and literary words, which is one reason some people wrongly think they come from Sanskrit.

The two languages have their own [[dialect|dialects]] too. Kannada spoken in Mangaluru sounds different from Kannada spoken in Dharwad, and Telugu in Hyderabad differs from Telugu along the coast.

sec.h: One script that split in two

sec.t:
The oldest surviving book in Kannada is the *Kavirajamarga*, a guide to poetry written around 850 CE at the court of the [[@rashtrakutas|Rashtrakuta]] king Amoghavarsha I. In the 12th century, [[@basavanna|Basavanna]] and other saints wrote *vachanas*, short sayings in everyday Kannada that people still quote.

In Telugu, the poet Nannaya began translating the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] in the 11th century, and he is often called the *Adi Kavi*, the first poet. Krishnadevaraya, the great emperor of [[@vijayanagara|Vijayanagara]] in the early 1500s, wrote poetry in Telugu himself.

Telugu also became a language of music. Tyagaraja, one of the most famous composers of [[@carnatic-hindustani|Carnatic music]], wrote most of his songs in Telugu in the 18th and 19th centuries. Because so many Telugu words end in vowels, they flow easily when sung. Some people call Telugu "the Italian of the East" for this reason, a phrase usually credited to a European traveller of the 1400s.

Kannada and Telugu are not museum pieces. They have huge film industries, newspapers, websites and songs. Kannada writers have won the Jnanpith, India's highest literary award, many times. The poet Kuvempu wrote Karnataka's state song, and the Telugu writer Viswanatha Satyanarayana was the first Telugu writer to receive the Jnanpith. Telugu is also one of the fastest-growing languages in the USA, where many families from Andhra Pradesh and Telangana have settled.

text: When you learn to write, you start by copying letter shapes from your teacher or a book. But as you practise, your brain turns writing into an automatic set of movements, a bit like riding a bicycle. Those movements depend on your hand size, your muscles, how you grip the pencil, your speed and many tiny habits you pick up along the way.

No two people learn in exactly the same way. By the time you are about 10 or 11, your handwriting is a mix of what you were taught and how your own body moves. Just like [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]], no two people's handwriting is exactly the same, even if they were taught side by side.

st.prompt: If you write your name with your other hand, your foot or a pen in your mouth, what happens?

options.t: It is messier, but the shapes still look like your usual handwriting
It looks completely different every time
You can't write at all

st.reveal: Your brain stores handwriting as a plan of movements, not as instructions for one hand. It can send that plan to different muscles. The result is shaky, but the letter shapes, slant and spacing are often recognisably yours.

sec.t:
Even [[@twins|identical twins]], who share the same [[gene|genes]], write differently. They may hold their pencils differently, copy different friends or pick up different habits. One twin might be left-handed and the other right-handed.

Your handwriting also changes during your life. It settles in your teens, may get faster and messier as an adult, and often becomes shakier in old age. Illness, tiredness and even the weather can change how it looks on a given day.

Forensic document examiners study handwriting to help solve crimes and court cases. They compare a suspicious signature or letter with samples of someone's known writing. They look at hundreds of tiny details, such as how letters join, where the pen starts and stops, and how hard it presses.

Forgers often copy the shape of a signature but write slowly and carefully. That can leave shaky lines and blunt starts and ends, which real fast writing doesn't have. Examiners use [[microscope|microscopes]] and special lights to spot these clues.

When India became a [[republic|republic]] in 1950, its [[@constitution|Constitution]] was written out by hand. The calligrapher Prem Behari Narain Raizada wrote the English version in flowing italic script. The Hindi version was hand-lettered by another calligrapher, Vasant Krishan Vaidya. Raizada worked for about six months and asked for no payment, only that he could sign his name on every page.

In the USA, the Declaration of Independence of 1776 was also handwritten, by a clerk named Timothy Matlack. His careful writing is on the copy displayed in Washington, DC, though the famous signatures, such as John Hancock's large one, belong to the signers themselves.

With phones and keyboards everywhere, some people ask whether children still need to learn handwriting. A 2024 study in Norway used caps fitted with [[sensor|sensors]] to record brain activity. It found that writing by hand activated more connections across the brain than typing, which may help with learning and memory.

In 2023, California passed a law bringing cursive, or joined-up handwriting, back into primary schools. Many Indian schools still teach both print and cursive in English, as well as handwriting in Hindi or a regional script.

For some people, handwriting is an art. [[@calligraphy|Calligraphy]], beautiful writing, is treasured in Chinese, Arabic, Japanese, Indian and European cultures. Calligraphers practise for years to control every curve and line.

Your everyday handwriting doesn't have to be beautiful, but it is uniquely yours. And it all began thousands of years ago when people first pressed marks into clay with reeds, part of the long story of [[@writing-tools|writing tools]].
